strengths: Addresses an important question: what multimodal contrastive learning recovers when modalities contain related but nonidentical latent factors.

The proposed CLIP postprocessing is simple, and experiments cover four backbones, multiple shot counts, domain shifts, and 11 few-shot benchmarks. Table 2 reports an improvement in ViT-B/16 target-average accuracy from 32.51% to 37.13%.
Synthetic experiments examine several distributional mismatches with repeated runs. Appendix P additionally provides quantitative latent-recovery results on Multimodal3DIdent.
weaknesses: The central proofs rely on a false Lemma 2 (Appendix D.1). It claims that the minimum normalized loss is zero and requires paired embeddings to coincide almost surely. Under the finite-concentration vMF model, latent pairs have full joint support, so this equality forces constant representations, contradicting uniformity and recovery. Moreover, with τ=1/k, identity latent encoders attain normalized loss −2I(zx;zt)<0, approximately −0.421 for k=1 on the circle. Consequently, the bridge used to prove Theorems 4.1–4.2 is not established.

The convex-body proof introduces another substantive error: Eq. (43) treats p(zt) as exactly uniform, whereas Lemma 3 establishes only convergence as λ approaches zero. For fixed positive λ, boundary-dependent normalization generally produces a nonuniform marginal, invalidating the exact cross-entropy reduction. Corollary 2 also omits the restriction to ℓp metrics with p≠2 introduced in Appendix E.2; Euclidean balls admit arbitrary rotations, preventing permutation-only identifiability.

The ICA-based component-wise guarantee conflicts with the spherical assumptions. A uniformly distributed spherical vector has dependent Cartesian coordinates and is rotationally invariant, so FastICA cannot identify a preferred orthogonal basis. The observation that the sphere has M−1 intrinsic dimensions does not resolve this incompatibility. Appendix O also labels arbitrary orthogonal mixing as component-wise disentanglement, although such mixing generally entangles individual factors.

The downstream experiments do not isolate disentanglement from preprocessing. Appendix K uses different retained dimensions for ICA and PCA+ICA, without matched PCA-only and whitening-only controls. Within a fixed whitened subspace, an L2-regularized linear probe is invariant to ICA's orthogonal rotation, so classification gains cannot establish that this rotation provides useful disentanglement. Furthermore, Appendix K's regression predicts learned features from true factors; high R² can therefore occur for rank-deficient representations and does not establish invertible latent recovery.

The claimed generality beyond DAGs is insufficiently demonstrated. The restrictive single-kernel latent distributions are not shown to represent the heterogeneous, opposing causal mechanisms motivating the paper. Nor does the manuscript establish why DAG models augmented with latent context variables are inadequate. Much of the subsequent identifiability machinery explicitly follows Zimmermann et al. (2021), making a valid multimodal extension essential to the novelty claim.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement: synthetic sample sizes and optimization schedules, the data used to fit ICA/PCA, and uncertainty across downstream few-shot runs are insufficiently specified. Table 2 also reports the RN101 baseline target average as 20.03%, although its four entries average 22.03%, overstating that comparison.
